outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 bears on whether infinitely many Pell numbers are prime. The in-window papers found concern Pell's equation, the largest prime factor of k-generalized Pell numbers, and a primality test built on Pell's cubic; none claims, proves, or refutes infinitude, and no source found calls the question settled. The only Pell-prime events located are instance records from 2001 and 2004 and a 2009 index search, all before the window.
problem_asks: (1) The Pell numbers P_n, in the standard indexing P_0 = 0, P_1 = 1, P_n = 2P_(n-1) + P_(n-2) (terms 0, 1, 2, 5, 12, 29, 70, ...), and the notion of a Pell prime: a Pell number that is prime. (2) Whether there are infinitely many Pell primes, i.e. whether infinitely many indices n give a prime P_n. This is a single existence-of-infinitely-many question; a finite list of instances does not answer it. The statement names no other sequence, so Pell-Lucas numbers are not asked about; the standard usage (OEIS A086383, MathWorld, Wikipedia) is the Pell numbers.

events.what_happened: MathWorld's table of the largest known (probable) Pell primes credits D. Broadhurst and P. Walker with index 13339 (5106 digits), dated Jul. 2001. MathWorld's Pell Number entry calls index 13339 the largest proven prime. Index 13339 is listed in OEIS A096650. The primary source for the 2001 computation was not located. Pre-window; recorded because it is a prime-Pell instance.
events.delivers: One more prime Pell number, P_13339 (5106 digits), with prime index, under the P_0 = 0 convention. It is one instance of a prime Pell number. It does not establish, and does not bear on, whether there are infinitely many.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: this adds an instance, not a bound on the count.
events.directly_checkable: Checkable only by computer: a primality certificate for P_13339. Not checked here; no certificate was located.
events.doubts: Source discrepancy, not a doubt about the arithmetic: the MathWorld text calls 13339 the largest proven prime, but the status column of the MathWorld table I read says 'Not stated' for that row.
events.direction: Adds one prime Pell number to the known list. Cuts toward the existence of prime Pell numbers, not toward their infinitude.
events.object: The Pell number at index 13339, a 5106-digit prime (P_13339 with P_0 = 0; index shifts under the alternative P_0 = 1 convention). It is an explicit number, so its primality is a specific claim, not a non-constructive existence result.

events.what_happened: T. D. Noe reported a probable prime Pell number at index 90197 (34525 digits). MathWorld lists it in its table dated Sep. 2004 as the largest known (probable) Pell prime. OEIS A096650 records Noe's additions of 17 Aug 2004 and 13 Sep 2004, and states that indices above 523 give probable primes, not proven primes. Pre-window.
events.revisions: OEIS A096650: terms added 17 Aug 2004 and 13 Sep 2004 (T. D. Noe). Last revision date not shown on the entry; the OEIS footer date is for the site snapshot.
events.delivers: One more prime-index Pell number, P_90197, of 34525 digits, given as a probable prime (PRP) only. It is an instance and a probabilistic one; it does not bear on infinitude.
events.directly_checkable: Checkable only by computer, as a probable-prime test on P_90197. Not run here.
events.doubts: Probable-prime status only (OEIS and MathWorld both say so), not a proven prime. No specific reason to think the test was wrong was found.
events.direction: Adds one probable prime Pell number. Cuts toward the existence of prime Pell numbers only; no bearing on infinitude.
events.object: The Pell number at index 90197, a 34525-digit probable prime (PRP), reported as the largest known probable Pell prime. Explicit number; the primality claim is probabilistic.

events.what_happened: E. W. Weisstein's MathWorld note, dated 21 Mar 2009, reports no Pell prime indices below 188856 beyond those listed. OEIS A096650 (T. D. Noe, 2004) states a search bound of 100000. Pre-window. A computational search to a bound.
events.delivers: Finite computational statement: no further prime Pell indices below 188856 as of March 2009. It covers finitely many instances.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. A search to a bound says nothing about indices beyond the bound.
events.directly_checkable: Checkable by computing P_n up to 188856 and testing primality. The method and code were not located.
events.direction: Finite search with no new prime index in range. Does not cut toward or against infinitude.

events.what_happened: Delmastro and Gomis, 'Symmetries of Abelian Chern-Simons Theories and Arithmetic' (arXiv:1904.12884, v1 29 Apr 2019; v2 11 Jan 2021). A search excerpt of the body reports a conjecture that a quadratic-type polynomial generates infinitely many 'Pell' values in the authors' own sense, that it follows from Hardy-Littlewood conjecture F, and that it was checked for k up to 10^9. The body was not opened; I read only the abstract page, which does not define 'Pell'. Pre-window.
events.revisions: v1 29 Apr 2019; v2 revised 11 Jan 2021 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Nothing about the Pell numbers. It is a namesake: a conjecture about a different 'Pell' integer family in Chern-Simons arithmetic. The authors describe it as open.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, as a different question.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against the Pell-number question. It is recorded because the name collides and the later pass should not conflate them.

events.what_happened: Hone, Jeffery and Selcoe, 'On a family of sequences related to Chebyshev polynomials' (arXiv:1802.01793, v1 6 Feb 2018; v3 revised 23 Jul 2018). The abstract proves that for a dilated Chebyshev family of linear recurrences the sequence contains at most one prime for some parameter values, and conjectures that for all other parameter values the sequence contains infinitely many primes. Pell numbers are not named, and the abstract does not say whether they fall in the class.
events.delivers: A general conjecture, not a result: for a class of linear recurrences (Lehmer-type), infinitely many primes for all parameters outside one dilated-Chebyshev family, which has at most one prime. It establishes nothing about the Pell numbers. My inference, not stated by the paper's abstract, is that the Pell numbers are a Lehmer sequence and so may lie in the conjectured class; this was not verified.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many Pell numbers are prime. A general class-level conjecture does not decide the Pell case.
events.direction: Conjectural and general. Points toward infinitely many primes for most parameter values, but gives no Pell-specific statement.

events.what_happened: Broderius and Greene, 'Lucas sequences containing few primes', Fibonacci Quarterly 59(2), pp. 136-144 (2021). The paper gives two families of Lucas sequences that contain only finitely many primes, and conjectures that all other Lucas sequences without obvious obstructions contain infinitely many primes. I read the abstract summary on the UMN listing; the family conditions on P and Q were not readable (the Fibonacci Quarterly PDFs failed to open). Pre-window; the 2021 date is the journal's, and no earlier preprint was found.
events.delivers: Finitely many primes for two families of Lucas sequences U_n(P,Q), with the family conditions not read. For the Pell numbers, which are U_n(2,-1), coverage by either finite family is not established. The conjecture of infinitude for the remaining Lucas sequences is not proved.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many Pell numbers are prime. This is open unless (P,Q) = (2,-1) lies in one of the two finite families, in which case the answer would be no. That check was not completed.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper. Refereeing of this paper was not verified in this run.

events.direction: Finitely many primes for some Lucas sequences; infinitude conjectured for the rest. Whether this cuts for or against the Pell case depends on the family conditions, which were not read.

events.what_happened: Herbert Batte, 'On the Largest Prime factor of the k-generalized Pell numbers' (arXiv:2504.19052, submitted 26 Apr 2025, single version). It proves that for n >= 4 the largest prime factor of the k-generalized Pell numbers (k >= 2, with k = 2 the classical Pell numbers) exceeds (1/104) log log n, and identifies all k-generalized Pell numbers whose largest prime factor is at most 7.
events.revisions: v1 only, 26 Apr 2025 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A lower bound on the largest prime factor of k-generalized Pell numbers, and a finite list of those with largest prime factor at most 7. It is about the largest prime factor of P_n, not about whether P_n is prime.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against the question: it measures a different quantity (largest prime factor).

events.what_happened: Luca Di Domenico and Nadir Murru, 'Novel performant primality test on a Pell's cubic' (arXiv:2411.01638, submitted 3 Nov 2024). It introduces a deterministic primality test for integers below 2^32, based on the Pell's cubic, with operations growing linearly in bit-length. The paper's 'Pell-X, Pell-Y, Pell-Z' sequences are third-order recurrences, not the classical Pell numbers.
events.delivers: A primality test for arbitrary integers (deterministic below 2^32). It does not show that any Pell number is prime, and it does not address infinitude.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against the question: it is primality testing, a different question.

events.what_happened: Bogdan Dumitru and Mihai Prunescu, 'Straight-line programs for the solutions of Pell's equation' (arXiv:2609.28649, submitted 23 Sep 2026, single version). The paper constructs fixed straight-line programs for the least nontrivial solution of x^2 - d y^2 = 1 and gives related formulas. It does not concern Pell numbers or their primality. The acknowledgement says: 'This paper was produced in an AI-assisted workflow.' and 'AI assistants helped explore candidate constructions, draft proofs, and write software for numerical experiments.' No system is named. Read from the arXiv HTML rendering; the PDF did not open.
events.revisions: v1 only, 23 Sep 2026 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Computational constructions for Pell's equation x^2 - d y^2 = 1. Nothing about whether Pell numbers are prime.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, as a different question.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against the question. Recorded because it is in-window, Pell-named, and AI-disclosed; the AI involvement is not on the Pell-prime question.

events.what_happened: Dowdall, Mattman, Meek and Solis, 'On the Harary-Kauffman Conjecture and Turk's Head Knots' (arXiv:0811.0044, submitted 31 Oct 2008 per the arXiv listing; the abstract page reads 1 Nov 2008). The abstract says the proof 'rests on the observation that these knots have prime determinant only for THK(m,2) when P_m is a Pell prime'. This is the only hit for the quoted phrase 'Pell primes' on arXiv. Pre-window.
events.delivers: Uses the Pell-prime property as a hypothesis on indices in a knot-determinant argument. It says nothing about how many Pell primes exist.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, as a different question.
events.direction: Neither cuts for nor against infinitude. It is a use of the term, not a result about Pell primes.

summary: Found nothing in the window that moves the question. Pell primes are Pell numbers P_n (P_0 = 0, P_1 = 1) that are prime. The Wikipedia Pell number article (opened; the 'Primes and squares' section lists the first prime terms and the prime indices, and states that a prime P_n needs n prime) does not say whether infinitely many exist. OEIS A086383 and A096650 (opened today) and MathWorld's PellPrime page (opened) give the terms and indices and no conjecture either way. The largest records there are a proven prime at index 13339 (Broadhurst and Walker, Jul 2001) and a probable prime at index 90197 (Noe, Sep 2004), with a 2009 search finding no further indices below 188856; nothing newer appears in OEIS as of today. Searches for AI involvement (eight queries pairing the name with AI, lab, prover, Erdos-tracker and disclosure terms, plus the AI-related arXiv abstract checks) found none specific to Pell primes. The AI-disclosed Pell paper in the neighbourhood, arXiv:2609.28649, is about Pell's equation and names no system. Close calls: (a) Broderius-Greene 2021 gives finitely many primes for two families of Lucas sequences and conjectures infinitude otherwise. The Pell numbers are U_n(2,-1), a Lucas sequence, and I could not read the family conditions, so I cannot say the Pell case is excluded. If it is inside a finite family, the answer to the question is already no (a pre-window event), which makes this the most consequential check. (b) Hone, Jeffery and Selcoe 2018 conjecture infinitude for Lehmer-type sequences outside one family. Pell numbers are a Lehmer sequence by the usual definition (my inference), but the abstract does not name them. (c) The 2019 Delmastro-Gomis 'Pell' conjecture is a namesake and is not about Pell numbers. (d) The MathWorld table and text disagree on whether 13339 is 'proven'. (e) The indices depend on the indexing convention; MathWorld notes P_0 = 1 is also used. Dead ends: the arXiv search for the quoted phrase 'Pell primes' returns one 2008 paper (above), for 'prime Pell numbers' zero, and for 'Pell prime' (unquoted) 37 hits, of which the in-window ones (2504.19052, 2501.01667, 2411.11103, 2503.21485, 2608.23418, 2608.30389, 2610.04254) concern Pell or Pell-type equations or Lucas congruences and not the primality of Pell numbers. Recent AI results found by search (OpenAI and other prime-gap claims in 2026, Erdos-problem solutions, DeepMind Aletheia, FrontierMath) concern other problems, and none names a Pell-prime result. The AI tracker and Erdos searches gave no Pell-prime hit. No source said 'open' or 'settled' for this question within the window; I infer it is open from the absence of any claim, not from a source that says so.
competing_reading: If the Broderius-Greene families cover (P,Q) = (2,-1), the question already has a negative answer from a 2021 event, which would count as settled before the window. Alternatively, the Hone-Jeffery-Selcoe conjecture (infinitude for Lehmer-type sequences outside one family) could be read as an expected yes that the question's own community treats as settled in direction. Neither reading is supported by a Pell-specific statement in any source read.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The theorem conditions of Broderius and Greene (Fibonacci Quarterly 59(2), 2021, pp. 136-144) and whether (P,Q) = (2,-1) lies in either finite family. (2) The parameter setup of arXiv:1802.01793, to see whether the Pell sequence is in the conjectured class. (3) A proof that infinitely many P_n are prime, or that only finitely many are. None was found. (4) The frozen 26 Jan 2024 Wikipedia list bullet, to confirm it links to the Pell number article and reads as the task statement does.
